| [LIT-037](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-037.md) v3 | The Open Systems View | Cuffaro et al. (2021), [ARXIV-2112.11095](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11095). The paper argues philosophically, not formally, that the quantum theory of open systems "GT" is more fundamental than standard closed-system quantum theory "ST". GT treats states as density operators that evolve, in general, non-unitarily, and it admits not-completely-positive maps. The ontic and epistemic cases each win only on a second, interpretation- or practice-laden criterion: OntFund-2 and EpFund-2. On the first, formal criteria (OntFund-1, EpFund-1) the two frameworks tie, and the authors say so because Stinespring dilation and dropping the Lindblad terms translate in both directions (§4.1, §4.2.1). Explanatory fundamentality is granted only deflationarily (ExFund-1), and the authors recommend dropping the notion (§4.2.2). The step from there to "the open systems view is fundamental tout court" (§4.3) rests on the special sciences and on "there are no other options". | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-077); worth reading as the clearest statement of the "open systems view" and of the distinction between a view, a framework, a theory and a model (§2, §4.1, §5.2). Read it knowing that its fundamentality verdict is carried by interpretive premises (OntFund-2, EpFund-2) and a deflationary step, not by any formal asymmetry between the frameworks. |
| [LIT-045](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-045.md) v3 | Structural Realism | Ladyman (2007), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/structural-realism/>. The entry presents structural realism (Worrall 1989) as the attempt to keep both the no-miracles argument and the pessimistic meta-induction: what survives theory change, and what we are entitled to believe, is a theory's mathematical or relational structure. It then separates an epistemic version (we can know only structure) from an ontic version (structure is all there is). The entry presents structural realism (Worrall 1989) as the attempt to keep both the no-miracles argument and the lesson of theory change. What is retained, and what we are entitled to believe, is structure, understood by ontic structuralists as modal structure. It sorts the view into an epistemic form, which falls to the Newman/Demopoulos–Friedman triviality result when stated as a Ramsey sentence (§3.2), and an ontic form with seven distinguishable theses, from eliminativism about individuals to "objects are constructs" (§4). The ontic form is motivated by quantum non-individuality and entanglement, gauge symmetry and the hole argument. The entry closes with seven objections, each answered in the author's own voice (§5). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-038.md)); the standard map of the structural-realism literature, written by the founder of OSR. Read §2 for the theory-change argument, §3.2 for the Newman problem and §4's seven OSR theses. Treat §5's rebuttals as the author's position, not as the field's settled view. |
| [LIT-062](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-062.md) v3 | On the reality of the quantum state | Pusey et al. (2011), [ARXIV-1111.3328](https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.3328). Take pure states \|ψ0⟩, \|ψ1⟩ with \|⟨ψ0\|ψ1⟩\| = cos θ. Assume (a) a model assigns each preparation a distribution µ_i(λ) over physical states, (b) n independent preparations yield the product distribution µ_{x1}(λ1)⋯µ_{xn}(λn), and (c) outcome probabilities depend only on (λ1, …, λn). If the model's predictions are within ε of quantum theory, then D(µ0, µ1) ≥ 1 − 2ε^{1/n} for any n with 2^{1/n} − 1 ≤ tan(θ/2) (Eq. 7, App. B). At ε = 0 the distributions for distinct pure states cannot overlap on a set of non-zero measure, so Harrigan–Spekkens ψ-epistemic models are ruled out. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-030); the founding ψ-ontology theorem. It is short, fully proved (App. A–B), and still the reference that every later ψ-epistemic/ψ-ontic argument, including LIT-007 §I.C and LIT-090, positions itself against. Read it with its assumption (b)–(c) in view, since that is where every response pushes. |

| [LIT-096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md) | What Is It Like to Be a Bat? | Nagel (1974), [DOI-10.2307/2183914](https://doi.org/10.2307/2183914). An organism has conscious states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism. That subjective character belongs to a type of point of view, and it is left out by every functional, intentional or causal analysis, since each is compatible with its absence. Reduction elsewhere moves away from a point of view toward the objective; here that move leads away from the thing being explained. So physicalism may be true, but we have no conception of how it could be. Nagel proposes an "objective phenomenology" that would describe experience to beings who cannot have it. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-089); the source of the "something it is like" criterion of consciousness that the record's AI-consciousness work (LIT-056) adopts as its target, and of the argument that no functional analysis can settle whether that criterion is met. |

Stage 1 is coordination in *collections* (pairwise, "aggregative" interactions of co-located individuals). The paper argues that "naturalizing teleology" serves at least two relatively autonomous projects with different success criteria. One is scientific: whether an organism-centred account improves biology, which requires operationalisable models that may trade truth for usefulness.
